query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the HVAF-i7 spray parameters to achieve higher particle velocity – specifically by setting a nozzle-to-substrate distance in the range of 300–350 mm – will improve deposition efficiency and allow FeCoNiCrAl bond coats to reach a sufficient thickness while maintaining low as-sprayed oxidation and good adhesion.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl powder (15–45 μm feedstock) deposited via the HVAF-i7 torch that produces acceptable coating quality but yields an inadequate coating thickness on bond-coat components (including in tight, 120 mm internal diameter geometries).
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 deposition process to increase the in-flight particle velocity by tuning spray parameters – for example, by setting an optimal spray distance (300–350 mm) and modifying fuel/oxygen flows to boost momentum transfer – thereby providing the kinetic energy necessary to deposit thicker layers.
generation.conditions: Deposition under conditions relevant to high-temperature bond-coat service (thermal barrier environments) and on substrates with confined geometries (internal diameters of approximately 120 mm), where the spray environment is controlled for minimal oxidation and high adhesion.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy leads to better particle flattening, improved splat formation, and higher deposition efficiency, which in turn facilitates the buildup of a thicker, dense, and adherent coating.
generation.mechanism: By increasing particle velocity, the HEA powder particles attain greater momentum during in-flight flight. This enhanced kinetic energy promotes more efficient flattening and bonding upon impact. As a result, thicker layers can accumulate with minimal in-spray oxidation, preserving the integrity and high-temperature durability of the bond coat.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (HVAF-i7 deposition using 15–45 μm feedstock at non-optimized parameters), the modified process will produce a significantly thicker, adherent bond coat that retains low oxidation and meets the service requirements under high-temperature thermal-barrier conditions.
generation.baseline: FeCoNiCrAl bond coats deposited using the HVAF-i7 torch with conventional 15–45 μm powder feedstock and standard spray parameters, which yield acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the process adjustments correctly increase particle velocity without inducing detrimental effects such as excessive oxidation or particle breakup. Deposition in very confined geometries may require further process tuning.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies on conventional MCrAlY coatings suggest benefits from higher particle velocity and specific spray distances, the exact quantitative improvement in coating thickness and the avoidance of oxidation in the HVAF-i7 system remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeCoNiCrAl coatings using the HVAF-i7 system: one set using the standard spray parameters (as per the current baseline) and a second set with the optimized parameters (adjusted nozzle-to-substrate distance of 300–350 mm and improved particle velocity settings). All other variables (feedstock size, composition, substrate preparation) are held constant. Compare the coating thickness, adhesion, and oxidation content between the two sets.
measurements: Coating thickness (via cross-sectional optical or electron microscopy)
Deposition efficiency (mass gain per unit area)
Oxidation level (using EDS or XRD analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized process does not result in a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (with maintained low oxidation and adhesion comparable to or better than the baseline), or if the intervention leads to degraded properties (e.g., increased oxidation or poor adhesion), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.
